seoTitle: Post Aura: website, search and an AI tagger
description: How I am building a Mumbai post production startup from scratch: the research, a website in five versions with search built in, and an AI footage tagger.
deck: Building a startup from scratch: the research, a website in five versions, its search layer and an AI footage tagger.
summary: A post production startup in Mumbai started from a single file wireframe and a pitch built on cost. Its editors tag every clip by hand in Premiere Pro, and those tags stay locked in project files that DaVinci Resolve never sees.

I researched the market, put five versions of the website live on test addresses over four days, with search built in from the first, and built an AI tagger that writes the studio's own tags into each video file.

Twelve days after the wireframe, the tagger's first production test tagged 10 real clips with no failures, on the Gemini fallback model. Its schedule was left paused, the editor tools wait on a test inside the apps, and the site waits on a domain.

offer.who: Post production studios and in house video teams that keep footage on Google Drive and edit in Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve.
offer.gets: New clips in your shared folders tagged on a schedule from your own classification sheet: year, country, place and camera from the folder path, the rest from five frames. The tags are written into each file, a review sheet sends your fixes back into the clips, and a read only check shows what the robot can open before it writes anything.
offer.needs: A Google Cloud project with billing, Claude Haiku 5.5 enabled in Vertex AI or the Gemini fallback until it is, MP4 or MOV footage in Drive folders you can share, and your classification sheet.
offer.setup: One deploy command from me, then you share your folders and your sheet. It runs on your own Google Cloud bill. Before the schedule goes on, we tag a sample of your clips and test the Premiere and Resolve steps with your editors.
offer.also: The research, the website and its search layer are an offer of their own, built the way this page shows. Ask about any of it in the same email.

beats.h3: A tagger that uses the studio's own words

sentences.t: At the kickoff I learned how the editors work.
They tag every clip by hand in Premiere Pro, and those tags live inside the project file, so DaVinci Resolve never sees them.
Six builds over four days took the tagger from a local tool to a private cloud service.
On 24 Oct it tagged 10 real clips with no failures.
That run used the Gemini fallback, which works without the manual step that turns Claude on in Vertex AI.

line.t: Year, country, place and camera from the folder path, five frames to Claude Haiku 5.5, answers limited to the tag list, XMP keywords written into the file and a CSV for Resolve.

My first demo used made up folders, so I rebuilt it on five Wikimedia Commons clips with folder paths taken from each clip's page. A person checked every tag: 25 of 33 right, 6 wrong, 2 debatable. On this timelapse the sunrise was not visible in the five frames, and still frames could not show that it was a timelapse.

line.t: A private Cloud Run service built to run every 30 minutes with nothing installed on editors' machines, plus a Premiere panel and a Resolve script. Three review rounds found 38, 13 and 13 issues, all fixed, and 259 checks passed.

sentences.t: The wireframe sold the studio on cost.
I ran five research tracks with 96 sources, then had three critic personas read the plan: a UK luxury hotel's head of brand, a creative director and a fact checker.
The research and the critiques ran as AI agent workflows that I directed and checked.
What came back changed what the site says.

Reviews ran in rounds.

Since then I give reviewers the client's source copy first.

tags-that-travel.h2: Tags that travel with the file

expected.t: Speed up tagging inside Premiere Pro, where the editors already work: fill the studio's custom columns faster, or lean on the AI search built into Premiere and Resolve.

sentences.t: Premiere keeps custom column values inside the project file.
They cannot be exported, Resolve never sees them, and the next project starts without them.
The built in AI search writes nothing into the files and does not know the studio's words.
It finds a shoot date or camera type only when the file already carries one.

turn.line: A clip goes to every project and every app. Its tags should go with it.

sentences.t: The tagger writes XMP keywords into each video file, as a new Drive revision.
Premiere can search them through its Dublin Core Subject column, a documented path not yet tried in the studio's own Premiere, and a script or a CSV import is built to carry them into Resolve.
The folder path already holds the year, country, place and camera, so the model only judges what five frames show.
It can only answer with words from the studio's list, and it is told that a wrong tag is worse than none.

the-tagger.h2: Sharing a folder is the setup

poster.alt: Sample data: a share dialog with a placeholder robot address and the Editor role, beside the folder's permission list with the robot added as an Editor.

caption.t: The tagger's own demo recorder, run on sample data from two local runs on 23 and 24 Oct 2026: five public Wikimedia Commons clips in a sample folder, tagged by Claude Haiku 5.5 through the command line. The people and the robot address are placeholders, and the tag words are withheld because they come from the studio's own list. The production test on studio footage used the Gemini fallback.

text.line: Step 1: before the share, the robot cannot open the sample folder.
Step 2: one share adds the robot account as an Editor.
Step 3: the robot lists every clip it can now open. None has tags yet.
Step 4: a preview run classifies every clip and writes nothing, then the real run writes the tags into each file: 5 clips, 0 failed, 35 seconds. The tag words are withheld.
Second run: every tagged clip skipped, so nothing is paid for twice.

lede.t: Adding footage takes one action: share a folder with the tagger's robot account as an Editor, and the next run finds it.

The year, country, place and camera come from the folder path, and the five frames decide the rest. A person checked the five frame tags against the frames and the clip's Commons description and marked all five right; no activity was picked, which is right for an empty beach.

sentences.t: Each run skips any clip whose checksum and tag version have not changed, so no clip is paid for twice.
Editors fix a tag in the review sheet, and the next run writes the fix back into the clip.
A failure on one file never stops a run; the next run tries that file again, up to three attempts in all.

sentences.t: Before the first write, the client's original revision is pinned.
After writing, the tagger compares the new file's duration and streams with the original and uploads nothing if they differ.
In Google Cloud the robot account holds one permission, to call the model, and no keys exist to leak.
A monthly budget alert watches the bill.
304 test functions cover the pipeline, from tagging and skipping on a rerun to writing back a human fix and isolating an error.
Three adversarial review rounds found 38, 13 and 13 issues, and every one was fixed.

limits.h3: What it does not do yet

The Premiere panel and the Resolve script are built but have not been run inside the apps.
The deployed version skips clips over 1,400 MB.

Accuracy on the studio's own footage waits on a 50 clip pilot; on five public clips, a person found 25 of 33 tags right with a draft list, and the results document marks 4 of 5 clips fully right with the studio's list.

the-math.h2: What hand tagging costs, worked out

img.alt: A dark results panel headed Second run, 0 clips tagged again, with five figures: 10 skipped as already tagged and unchanged, 0 human fixes written back, 0 failed, 6,595 and 147 tokens, and a cost of 0.07 rupees.

caption.t: The production test's second run skipped the 10 tagged clips, so none was paid for twice. The tokens and cost on screen are for one new clip it previewed without writing, priced at Claude Haiku 5.5 rates, though this run used the Gemini fallback.

lede.t: Nobody has timed the studio's editors yet, so I do not quote a saving. Here is the model instead, with every input in the open.

The model fees come from tokens I measured and Claude's published price.

sentences.t: Reviewers flag what they cannot check, so I now give them the client's own copy before they start.
A demo is only honest when every value in it comes from a source; my first one did not, so I rebuilt it on public clips.
And a measurement is only as good as the build it ran on: once a stale server answered a contrast check with the old build, so I now confirm which build is being served before I measure.
